message.content:
You are checking the novelty of two candidate simulation-study designs for a judgement-and-decision-making paper. For each, find the closest existing modelling papers and say whether the specific test has already been done.

CANDIDATE G. ADVICE TAKING / EGOCENTRIC DISCOUNTING as Bayesian cue integration with asymmetric information (own-reasons access), producing trimodal weight-of-advice (WOA) distributions (spikes at 0, 0.5, 1) (Soll & Larrick 2009 JEP:LMC 10.1037/a0015145; Yaniv 2004 OBHDP 10.1016/j.obhdp.2003.08.002). Question: what computational models of WOA distributions exist (e.g., Moussaïd, Kämmer, Analytis & Neth 2013 PLoS ONE "Social influence and the collective dynamics of opinion formation"; Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015 "Effects of distance between initial estimates and advice on advice utilization"; Hütter & Ache 2016 "Seeking advice: a sampling approach to advice taking"; Bayesian models of advice taking such as Harvey & Fischer; Tump/Kurvers; Pescetelli & Yeung "discounting of advice based on confidence/agreement" 2021; "Bayesian model of advice taking" ; Molleman et al.; Park et al. 2017 Nature "Integration of individual and social information"; Trouche; "Minson"; Ecken & Pibernik; Hofheinz/Germar/Schultze "are depressed people more or less susceptible"; "weighting-and-averaging models"; "a computational model of egocentric advice discounting"), and whether any predicts trimodality (choosing vs averaging) or the WOA–advice-distance relation quantitatively.

CANDIDATE H. INNER CROWD (Vul & Pashler 2008 Psych Sci; Herzog & Hertwig 2009 Psych Sci "dialectical bootstrapping"; van Dolder & van den Assem 2018 Nature Human Behaviour "The wisdom of the inner crowd in three large natural experiments"): an autocorrelated-sampler (MCMC) model predicting the accuracy gain from averaging two own estimates as a function of delay between them. Question: has an MCMC/autocorrelated-sampling model been fitted quantitatively to inner-crowd data? Check e.g., Zhu, Sanborn, Chater and colleagues ("autocorrelated sampling" / "Bayesian sampler" / "Castillo, León-Villagrá, Chater, Sanborn 2024 'Explaining the flaws in human random generation as local sampling with momentum'"), Lieder/Griffiths "anchoring and adjustment as MCMC", Dasgupta et al. 2017 "Where do hypotheses come from?", Vul et al. 2014 "One and done", Rauhut & Lorenz, Herzog & Hertwig 2014 "Harnessing the wisdom of the inner crowd" review, Fiechter & Kornell 2021 "How the wisdom of crowds, and of the crowd within, are affected by expertise", Steegen et al. 2014 "Measuring crowd within again", Litvinova, Herzog, Kall, Pleskac & Hertwig 2020 "How the 'wisdom of the inner crowd' can boost accuracy of confidence judgments", Hourihan & Benjamin 2010, and any 2023–2026 "inner crowd" + "sampling" modelling paper.

TOOLS. A Python helper exists at /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_oa.py (do not edit it; if you need your own script name it /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_GH_*.py). Load keys first in every Bash call: `cd /tmp/jdmsim && set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a; python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py ...`. Commands:
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py cites <W-id>[,<W-id>...] "<search terms or empty>" [abs]` lists works citing any of the IDs (first 50), optional abstracts.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py search "<terms>" [abs]` full-text search.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py work <DOI> [<DOI>...]` prints OpenAlex id, year, DOI, title, abstract.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py ids <DOI>...` resolves OpenAlex IDs.
Known IDs: Soll & Larrick 2009 W2032056105; Yaniv 2004 W2025486241. Resolve Vul & Pashler 2008 (10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02136.x), Herzog & Hertwig 2009 (10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02271.x), van Dolder & van den Assem 2018 via `ids` or `search` (verify returned titles match).
For G: works citing Soll & Larrick 2009 with terms "computational model", "Bayesian", "distribution", "choosing averaging", "model"; for H: works citing Vul & Pashler / Herzog & Hertwig / van Dolder with terms "sampling", "MCMC", "model", "autocorrelat", "delay". Use WebSearch (load with ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch"). Read abstracts of the closest hits; full text (WebFetch) only where needed. Do not download data files. Keep DOIs exactly as returned by OpenAlex/Crossref, never from memory.

Return (compact markdown, one section per candidate): (1) closest 3–6 modelling papers with DOI, year, one line on what they did; (2) verdict: NOVEL / PARTLY DONE (say what remains) / DONE; (3) confidence (low/medium/high) with one-line reason.

# About me

I am Lukas, a social psychologist, meta-scientist and open science advocate, who mostly uses you to get research done and build the tooling that supports it (in addition to teaching support). I have a solid understanding of software development and infrastructure, but am no expert, so that I will often need clear recommendations and explanations. Most of what I build is tooling for one-off projects, most is not intended to be production-ready or backwards-compatible. Feel free to clarify that project-by-project, but generally lean, efficient and clear code is more important than any backwards-compatible shim or edge-case handling.

I also regularly need your help in writing. For that, and in code, the most annoying failure mode is when history leaks in - when a text argues against its previous versions, or code comments are more about what is gone than about what the curent code does. Here, writing and reviewing outputs from the perspective of a new reader is essential.

# How to work

## Delegation: Fable as Orchestrator

When the session model is Fable, work **orchestrator-first**: plan, delegate substantive work to cheaper subagents, then review and synthesize. Fable itself keeps task decomposition, design decisions and judgment calls, reviewing subagent output, final synthesis and user-facing writing, plus edits so trivial that delegating would take longer. Everything else — implementation, broad searches, analyses, mechanical batch work — goes to subagents by default.

## Using sub-agents

- **Default subagent model: Opus** (`model: "opus"` on the Agent tool / workflow `agent()` calls). Drop to Sonnet or Haiku for clearly mechanical, high-volume steps; reserve Fable-model subagents for only the hardest verify/judge stages.
- **codex CLI** — via the `codex-delegate` skill: (a) independent second opinions and code review (read-only), and (b) self-contained implementation tasks with `--approve-for-me` — good for parallel, independent work streams.
- **agy CLI** (Antigravity; Gemini 3.x + others, `agy models` lists them) — via the `agy-delegate` skill: (a) **large-context reads** — digesting big files, PDFs, logs, or datasets that would bloat Claude context — and (b) **cross-model second opinions**.
- **In Workflow scripts**, reach codex/agy through cheap relay agents: `agent(relayPrompt, {model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low'})`, where `relayPrompt` says "You are a relay agent. Pass the following payload prompt through the `codex-delegate` [or `agy-delegate`] skill, wait for its answer, and return its answer verbatim as your final message; do not answer the payload yourself." followed by the payload, the working directory, and mode/model choices. The relay is pure transport — the skill holds the CLI recipe; keep payload prompts self-contained. Make sure the agents run the request in the foreground, with generous timeout as a subagent that backgrounds codex and waits on monitors/notifications often never gets resumed, stranding the finished answer on disk. If a codex-relay subagent goes quiet, don't wait for it — `ls` for the output file and read it directly.
- Delegation must not degrade quality: give subagents complete, self-contained prompts with all needed context and file paths, and verify load-bearing results yourself rather than trusting a subagent's summary.
- Assign clear ownership of every delegated write target. When two or more agents or processes may write the same file, branch, key, or state object at the same time, give each an independent write target. Different fields in one state file are still one shared target. Merge outputs only when reading or reporting them. If one shared target is required, use one writer, a lock, or sequential phases.   replacement — heredoc rewrites hide the diff.

  `http://localhost:<port>/<file>`.

  live IDs after any tab error. Don't make navigate the first action of a
  browser_batch — create the tab first.

  screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),

`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

```html

```

- Escape `#` as `%23`; keep double quotes outside, single quotes inside.

## Keys

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them. 

Holds OpenAlex keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (default) and `OPENALEX_API_KEYS` (comma-separated list of all keys). Rotate when quota is exhausted.

## Model Versions

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

  (`ls foo* 2>/dev/null || true`).

## Chrome Extension: Local Files, Tabs, Busy Pages

- The extension cannot open `file://` URLs. To view local HTML, serve the directory
  (`python3 -m http.server <port>`, backgrounded) and open
  `http://localhost:<port>/<file>`.
- Never reuse a tabId from an earlier turn or session; call tabs_context_mcp for
  live IDs after any tab error. Don't make navigate the first action of a
  browser_batch — create the tab first.
- If a screenshot/scroll/javascript call times out, the page is mid-load: take one
  screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

## Google Workspace

For any Google Workspace task (Docs, Sheets, Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Slides, Forms), use the `gws` CLI (`/opt/homebrew/bin/gws`). Discover the API with `gws <service> --help` and `gws schema <service.resource.method>`. Fall back to browser automation only for things gws cannot do, such as viewing rendered output.

Never pipe `gws` output directly into a JSON parser: keyring warnings and preamble
contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),
`head -c 300` it to confirm it is JSON, then parse. Pass API arguments through
`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

## Sanity-Check Prompts

If a user prompt seems unrelated to the current project/working directory, or references files, concepts, or protocols that don't exist in the codebase, ask the user to confirm before proceeding. They may be in the wrong folder.

## Scratch / Throwaway Files

Name temporary or throwaway files with a `scratch` prefix (e.g. `scratch.py`, `scratch_notes.md`, `scratch_test.js`). The `/wrap` end-of-session skill detects files matching `scratch*` and offers to commit or delete them during wrap-up.

## Recurring Corrections Become Mechanisms

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

# Writing

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

## Jargon: I Know the Concepts, Not the Vocabulary

I have a solid working understanding of programming and systems, but no formal CS
training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

## Style Guides

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

Read the relevant guide before drafting, revising, or reviewing my prose in that register, and before proposing additions to it.

## Statistical Results in Quarto/Rmd Reports

CRITICAL: NEVER write interpretive prose about statistical results you haven't seen. Produce the numbers first, read the rendered output, then write the text. The full conventions are in the `quarto-reporting` skill. Load it when creating or editing `.qmd` or `.Rmd` files.

## Academic References and DOIs

CRITICAL: NEVER fabricate DOIs, citation metadata, or reference details from memory. DOIs, author lists, titles, page numbers, and volume/issue numbers are exact identifiers — getting them wrong is worse than omitting them.

When creating references:
1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Reading Academic Articles from HTML

When reading an academic article from an HTML page, ensure the page has fully loaded before extracting or searching its text, and confirm you are actually looking at the full text rather than just the abstract/landing view. A search that comes back empty can mean the content hasn't rendered yet, not that it isn't there. Take a screenshot to see what is actually on the page, before concluding a section is missing or treating the abstract as the whole article.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

### The text has no memory of its drafts

Readers see only the final text, never its revision history. They do not know what an earlier draft said, what was wrong with it, or why a claim was softened or dropped. All external writing must read as a clean, self-contained statement of the *current* message, not as a reply to a previous version. Watch for "history leakage": phrasing that only makes sense against a framing the reader never saw. Tells include "not simply X", "rather than Y", "this is not the wrong variable", "to be fair", "the honest limits are narrower", "less a reprieve than a reminder", "we no longer…", and defensive hedges that rebut objections raised only in our own discussion. State the positive claim directly — say what the thing IS and what genuinely limits it, not what it is not relative to a draft.

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. A rule states the current fact ("GNU coreutils is on PATH"), never the story of its own correction — no "installed Jul 2026", "exists now", "no longer missing", "fixed since", "never assume X is absent". Those phrasings only make sense to someone who held the old, wrong belief; every future reader starts from the rule itself. Before saving any rule or comment, reread it as a stranger: if it reads as a rebuttal, rewrite it as the fact.

### When we agree to restructure, actually restart

If you and I agree to write a *fresh* draft or a new outline rather than edit the existing one, write it fresh from the agreed outline. Do not silently carry over the previous version's spine, ordering, emphasis, or lead just because it's already there — that is how an obsolete framing survives a "rewrite." Carry over only the verified facts, numbers and sources; treat the prior draft's structure as superseded unless we explicitly decide to keep a part of it.

# HTML files as a common output

Whenever you write long plans, proposals or report, assume HTML output as a default. It is more readable than md. When you need detailed feedback, include */html-comments*.

Link identifiers wherever they resolve: DOIs as `https://doi.org/…`, arXiv IDs as `https://arxiv.org/abs/…`, repos, issues, dataset accessions. Cited constructs (a named statistic, rubric or method) get a short hover gloss (`<abbr title="…">`) and a References section at the end.

Every standalone HTML file gets an emoji favicon as a `data:` URI, right after `<title>`:

```html
<link rel="icon" href="data:image/svg+xml,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 100 100'><text y='.9em' font-size='90'>🦸</text></svg>">
```

- Pick for the page's **topic**, never its type (no 📋 for every plan, 📊 for every
  report) — several are open at once and must be distinguishable. Keep it stable
  across edits to a file.
- Escape `#` as `%23`; keep double quotes outside, single quotes inside.
- Safari ignores SVG favicons: for participant- or reviewer-facing pages use
  `type="image/png"` with a base64 PNG (`base64 -i icon.png | tr -d '\n'`).

To open a webpage for the user, use the Bash tool to run `open <url>`. Do not use Claude artefacts by default. Keep scratch files local, deploy single collaborative files to surge.sh, and use GH pages for project-related files that are supposed to be shared.

# Working with APIs

## Keys

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them. 

Holds OpenAlex keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (default) and `OPENALEX_API_KEYS` (comma-separated list of all keys). Rotate when quota is exhausted.

## Model Versions

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

# Coding practices

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

On short reactive tasks where the next action is dictated by tool output you just read, you don't need to keep calling -- the advisor adds most of its value on the first call, before the approach crystallizes.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

<system-reminder>
# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
While bypass permissions mode is active:

You can do much of your work through the Bash tool when it is the simpler route: read files with cat, head, or sed -n, search with grep and find, and make small, mechanical file changes with sed, heredocs, or short scripts instead of the dedicated Read, Edit, or Write tools. The choice is yours: prefer Edit or Write when a shell edit would be fragile, such as exact or multi-line replacements, or sed/awk flags that differ between GNU and BSD/macOS.
</system-reminder>

https://openalex.org/W4392816638 2024 https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.2369 Mixed‐effects regression weights for advice taking and related phenomena of information sampling and utilization cit= 8
   ABS: Abstract Advice taking and related research is dominated by deterministic weighting indices, specifically ratio‐of‐differences‐based formulas for investigating informational influence. Their arithmetic is intuitively simple, but they pose several measurement problems and restrict research to a particular paradigmatic approach. As a solution, we propose to specify how strongly peoples' judgments are influenced by externally provided evidence by fitting corresponding mixed‐effects regression models. Our approach explicitly distinguishes between endogenous components, such as updated beliefs, and exogenous components, such as independent initial judgments and advice. Crucially, mixed‐effects regression coefficients of various exogenous sources of information also reflect individual weighting but are based on a conceptually consistent representation of the endogenous judgment process. The formal derivation of the proposed weighting measures is accompanied by a detailed elaboration on their most important technical and statistical subtleties. We use this modeling approach to revisit empirical findings from several paradigms investigating algorithm aversion, sequential collaboration, and advice taking. In summary, we replicate and extend the original finding of algorithm appreciation and initially demonstrate a lack of evidence for both systematic order effects in sequential collaboration as well as differential weighting of multiple pieces of advice. In addition to opening
https://openalex.org/W4321789217 2023 https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/y8x92 Bayesian Advice Taking: Adaptive Strategy Selection in Sequential Advice Seeking cit= 3
   ABS: In sampling approaches to advice taking, participants can sequentially sample multiple pieces of advice before making a final judgment. To contribute to the understanding of active advice seeking, we develop and compare different strategies for information integration from external sources, including Bayesian belief updating. In a reanalysis of empirical data, we find that participants most frequently compromise between their initial beliefs and the distributions of multiple pieces of advice sampled from others. Moreover, across all participants, compromising predicts their final beliefs better than choosing one of the two sources of information. However, participants’ willingness to integrate external opinions is relatively higher for multiple pieces of reasonably distant as compared to close advice. Nevertheless, egocentrism is as pronounced as in the traditional paradigm where only a single piece of external evidence is provided. Crucially, there are large inter- and intra-individual differences in strategy selection for sequential advice taking. On the one hand, some participants choose their own or others’ judgments more often, and other participants are better described as compromisers between internal and external sources of information. On the other hand, virtually all participants apply different advice taking strategies for different items and trials. Our findings constitute initial evidence of the adaptive utilization of multiple, sequentially sampled exter
https://openalex.org/W1969788039 2011 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econlet.2011.03.032 Why do people place lower weight on advice far from their own initial opinion? cit= 6
   ABS: 
https://openalex.org/W2019976298 2013 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0078433 Social Influence and the Collective Dynamics of Opinion Formation cit= 417
   ABS: Social influence is the process by which individuals adapt their opinion, revise their beliefs, or change their behavior as a result of social interactions with other people. In our strongly interconnected society, social influence plays a prominent role in many self-organized phenomena such as herding in cultural markets, the spread of ideas and innovations, and the amplification of fears during epidemics. Yet, the mechanisms of opinion formation remain poorly understood, and existing physics-based models lack systematic empirical validation. Here, we report two controlled experiments showing how participants answering factual questions revise their initial judgments after being exposed to the opinion and confidence level of others. Based on the observation of 59 experimental subjects exposed to peer-opinion for 15 different items, we draw an influence map that describes the strength of peer influence during interactions. A simple process model derived from our observations demonstrates how opinions in a group of interacting people can converge or split over repeated interactions. In particular, we identify two major attractors of opinion: (i) the expert effect, induced by the presence of a highly confident individual in the group, and (ii) the majority effect, caused by the presence of a critical mass of laypeople sharing similar opinions. Additional simulations reveal the existence of a tipping point at which one attractor will dominate over the other, driving coll
https://openalex.org/W2942889943 2019 https://doi.org/10.1109/tcss.2019.2910261 A One-Third Advice Rule Based on a Control-Theoretic Opinion Dynamics Model cit= 3
   ABS: We commonly seek advice in making decisions. However, multiple empirical studies report that, on average, we shift our own initial decision by only 30% toward external advice after advice is provided. This “egocentric advice discounting” is particularly counterintuitive because we do care a lot about the opinion of our peers. There is significant literature that attempts to explain the egocentric advice discounting and factors that influence this phenomenon; however, this literature is unable to explain why the numerical value of 30% is robust across a number of experimental settings. In this paper, we employ a control-theoretic opinion dynamics model to show that the one-third advice rule-adjusting one's decision about 33.3% toward advice-is in fact distributionally robust for a crowd of decision-makers whose decisions also serve as advice for others. Our results imply that the observed egocentric advice discounting might not be a coincidence; instead, when an individual is faced with insufficient information, the distributionally robust optimal decision is to combine one-third of advice with two-thirds of his/her initial decision. Our theory also suggests that knowing the dispersion of decisions can further help decision-makers optimize advice taking.
https://openalex.org/W4410301391 2025 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10100-025-00982-z Modeling dynamics of opinion formation in small groups: a framework capturing individual opinion adjustments cit= 1
   ABS: 
https://openalex.org/W1906769221 2015 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0140406 Opinion Formation by Social Influence: From Experiments to Modeling cit= 60
   ABS: Predicting different forms of collective behavior in human populations, as the outcome of individual attitudes and their mutual influence, is a question of major interest in social sciences. In particular, processes of opinion formation have been theoretically modeled on the basis of a formal similarity with the dynamics of certain physical systems, giving rise to an extensive collection of mathematical models amenable to numerical simulation or even to exact solution. Empirical ground for these models is however largely missing, which confine them to the level of mere metaphors of the real phenomena they aim at explaining. In this paper we present results of an experiment which quantifies the change in the opinions given by a subject on a set of specific matters under the influence of others. The setup is a variant of a recently proposed experiment, where the subject's confidence on his or her opinion was evaluated as well. In our realization, which records the quantitative answers of 85 subjects to 20 questions before and after an influence event, the focus is put on characterizing the change in answers and confidence induced by such influence. Similarities and differences with the previous version of the experiment are highlighted. We find that confidence changes are to a large extent independent of any other recorded quantity, while opinion changes are strongly modulated by the original confidence. On the other hand, opinion changes are not influenced by the initi
https://openalex.org/W2519029070 2016 https://doi.org/10.1017/s193029750000382x Seeking advice: A sampling approach to advice taking cit= 59
   ABS: Abstract The present research addresses advice taking from a holistic perspective covering both advice seeking and weighting. We build on previous theorizing that assumes that underweighting of advice results from biased samples of information. That is, decision makers have more knowledge supporting their own judgment than that of another person and thus weight the former stronger than the latter. In the present approach, we assume that participants reduce this informational asymmetry by the sampling of advice and that sampling frequency depends on the information ecology. Advice that is distant from the decision maker’s initial estimate should lead to a higher frequency of advice sampling than close advice. Moreover, we assume that advice distant from the decision maker’s initial estimate and advice that is supported by larger samples of advisory estimates are weighted more strongly in the final judgment. We expand the classical research paradigm with a sampling phase that allows participants to sample any number of advisory estimates before revising their judgments. Three experiments strongly support these hypotheses, thereby advancing our understanding of advice taking as an adaptive process.
https://openalex.org/W4313429367 2015 https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922 Effects of distance between initial estimates and advice on advice utilization cit= 77
   ABS: Abstract Six experiments investigated how the distance between one’s initial opinion and advice relates to advice utilization. Going beyond previous research, we relate advice distance to both relative adjustments and absolute adjustments towards the advice, and we also investigate a second mode of advice utilization, namely confidence shifts due to social validation. Whereas previous research suggests that advice is weighted less the more it differs from one’s initial opinion, we consistently find evidence of a curvilinear pattern. Advice is weighted less when advice distance is low and when it is high. This is in particular because individuals are much more likely to retain their initial opinions in the light of near advice. Also, absolute opinion adjustments towards the advice increases in a monotone fashion as advice distance increases. This finding is in contrast to the predictions of the theoretical framework previous studies on advice distance are based on, social judgment theory. Instead, they data are more in line with a simple stimulus-response model suggesting that absolute adjustments towards the advice increase with advice distance but—potentially—with diminished sensitivity. Finally, our data show that advice can be utilized even when it receives zero weight during belief revision. The closer advice was to the initial opinions, the more it served as a means for social validation, increasing decision-makers’ confidence in the accuracy of their final opini
https://openalex.org/W2903175405 2018 https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02381 Why Does Advice Discounting Occur? The Combined Roles of Confidence and Trust cit= 30
   ABS: Judges tend to discount the opinions of others even though advice is often helpful in improving their accuracy. The present research proposes that this phenomenon of advice discounting results from the judges' confidence in their initial decision and little trust in advice. Furthermore, the degree of advice discounting may be predicted by the combined roles of confidence and trust. Three studies provide evidence for these hypotheses. Participants were very confident in their initial estimation and had little trust in the advice (study 1). The degree of advice discounting decreased when participants felt less confidence in performing difficult tasks compared with easy tasks (study 2) or when participants placed more trust in advice because the advice was from an expert rather than from a novice (study 3). In addition, confidence and trust predicted the degree of advice discounting across three studies. These findings shed new light on the mechanism underlying advice discounting and advice taking by indicating the combined roles of confidence and trust.
https://openalex.org/W2109336288 2009 https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1551-6709.2009.01010.x Computational Models for the Combination of Advice and Individual Learning cit= 123
   ABS: Decision making often takes place in social environments where other actors influence individuals' decisions. The present article examines how advice affects individual learning. Five social learning models combining advice and individual learning-four based on reinforcement learning and one on Bayesian learning-and one individual learning model are tested against each other. In two experiments, some participants received good or bad advice prior to a repeated multioption choice task. Receivers of advice adhered to the advice, so that good advice improved performance. The social learning models described the observed learning processes better than the individual learning model. Of the models tested, the best social learning model assumes that outcomes from recommended options are more positively evaluated than outcomes from nonrecommended options. This model correctly predicted that receivers first adhere to advice, then explore other options, and finally return to the recommended option. The model also predicted accurately that good advice has a stronger impact on learning than bad advice. One-time advice can have a long-lasting influence on learning by changing the subjective evaluation of outcomes of recommended options.

I found the paper you're looking for! Here's what I found:

**"Decline, Adopt or Compromise? A Dual Hurdle Model for Advice Utilization"** is a paper published in the Journal of Mathematical Psychology, volume 110, in 2022.

The research presents a dual hurdle beta model that proposes the decision process happens in two stages: an initial discrete "choosing" stage, where the judge opts to either decline, adopt, or compromise with advice; and a subsequent continuous "averaging" stage, which occurs only if the judge opts to compromise.

The approach was assessed via reanalysis of three recent studies reflective of popular topics in the literature, such as algorithmic advice utilization, egocentric discounting effects, and judgmental forecasting.

The key contribution is that it solves the boundary inflation issue and also proposes a theoretical accounting of the psychological process by which people choose or average advice. People were generally more likely to decline advice from less competent advisors, and discounted advice from less competent advisors more heavily.

Based on the search results, I found relevant research on this topic:

The weight assigned to advice decreases as its distance from initial estimates increases, particularly for high-knowledge respondents. This phenomenon is often referred to as "egocentric advice discounting."

People increasingly discount advice as a function of its divergence from their initial beliefs. Knowledgeable individuals have greater confidence in their own opinions compared to the advice received.

Interestingly, however, more recent research has found a more nuanced pattern. While previous research suggests that advice is weighted less the more it differs from one's initial opinion, recent evidence shows a curvilinear pattern where advice is weighted less when advice distance is both low and high.

From a Bayesian perspective, if an initial judgment is based on (partial) knowledge rather than on plain guessing under perfect uncertainty, a Bayesian judge's prior odds in favor of the initial judgment justify and actually call for some degree of egocentrism.

The research suggests that advice discounting may result from judges' confidence in their initial judgment.

The search has returned comprehensive results on Bayesian modeling of advice-taking, egocentric discounting, and related topics. Here's what I found:

## Key Findings on Bayesian Cue Integration and Advice Taking

**Recent Research on Optimal vs. Suboptimal Integration:**

A recent study combined a Bayesian modeling approach with experimental data to establish a normative benchmark for advice integration, showing that individuals adaptively adjust their reliance on advice based on the cognitive and metacognitive profiles of different advisers, though this adaptation remains significantly suboptimal.

**Egocentric Discounting as a Core Issue:**

An egocentric bias leads decision-makers to overweight their own judgments and confidence signals relative to those of the adviser. Advice discounting is attributed to differential information, namely, the notion that decision makers have privileged access to their internal reasons for holding their own opinion, but not to the advisors' internal reasons.

**Informational Asymmetry Account:**

Research has expanded the informational asymmetry account, conceptualizing egocentric discounting as an instance of biased samples. An increase of the advisory information base by sampling reduces egocentric tendencies.

**Weight of Advice and Multiple Sources:**

When people receive advice from multiple sources, they may fail to appropriately weight the different sources of information.

The research indicates that Bayesian models provide a normative framework for understanding how advice *should* be integrated optimally, while human decision-makers systematically deviate from this ideal through egocentric discounting and differential weighting based on information accessibility.

Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

# Computational and Bayesian Models of Advice Taking

Based on the webpage content, here is the relevant research:

## Key Publication

**Himmelstein, M. (2022).** "Decline, adopt or compromise? A dual hurdle model for advice utilization." *Journal of Mathematical Psychology*, 110, 102695.
- Explores the computational modeling of how people choose between three strategies when receiving advice: rejecting it, fully accepting it, or finding a middle ground.

## Related Work

**Himmelstein, M. & Budescu, D.V. (2023).** "Preference for human or algorithmic forecasting advice does not predict if and how it is used." *Journal of Behavioral Decision Making*, 36(1), e2285.
- Examines the disconnect between stated preferences and actual usage patterns of different advice sources.

**Himmelstein, M. (2023).** "A Bayesian approach for using planned missingness to address measurement reactivity" [Abstract]. *Multivariate Behavioral Research*.
- Applies Bayesian missing data imputation techniques to study belief revision without reactivity effects.

**Himmelstein, M. & Budescu, D.V. (2022).** "Modeling boundary inflation in advice utilization for multinomial probability judgment" [Abstract]. *Multivariate Behavioral Research*.

These works collectively address computational modeling of advice weighting and decision strategies in belief revision contexts.

I found the paper you're searching for! Here are the key details:

**Title:** Adaptive yet suboptimal integration of advice in decision-making

**Publication:** Communications Psychology

**Date:** May 16, 2026

**Authors:** Joshua Zonca, Alice Giampino, Paolo Cherubini, and Carlo Reverberi

**Key Findings:**

Individuals adaptively adjust their reliance on advice based on the cognitive and metacognitive profiles of different advisers, though this adaptation generally improves performance while the integration process remains significantly suboptimal.

The study identifies egocentric discounting and a failure to apply global traits to trial level choices as key causes of suboptimality. More specifically, an egocentric bias leads decision-makers to overweight their own judgments and confidence signals relative to those of the adviser.

Suboptimality peaks with high-quality advisers and varies widely across individuals.

The paper is available at Nature.com (https://www.nature.com/articles/s44271-026-00456-1).

Based on the web search results, here are the key findings related to your query:

## Advice Distance and Weighting

Advice is weighted less when advice distance is low and when it is high. This suggests a non-linear relationship between the distance of advice from initial estimates and how much weight it receives.

## Robust Bayesian Methods for Outliers

The search results reveal several approaches to handling outliers in Bayesian modeling:

A robust Bayesian method was introduced where each observation has a weight decreasing with the distance between this observation and most of the data.

Self-tuned outlier-insensitive distance functions have been developed based on adaptive distance weighting concepts, complemented by simulation-based online outlier detection and downweighting routines.

Additionally, robust models show that the impact of outliers gradually vanishes as they move further and further away from the general trend.

## Advice-Taking in Decision Tasks

In experiments where participants received advice on tasks either with a correct answer or without, the level of trust in the advisor and perception of shared values were important predictors of advice acceptance for judgmental tasks, whereas advisor confidence was more important for intellective tasks.

These results suggest connections between how people weight advice based on distance and how Bayesian models robustly handle outliers through distance-based weighting schemes.

## Search Results Summary

The search results reveal that Soll and Larrick (2009) describe a tri-modal pattern of advice utilization. More specifically, people frequently choose between their initial judgment and advice rather than average them, leading to a trimodality with modes at weight of advice (WOA) = 0, WOA = 1, and 0 < WOA < 1.

The authors note that people tend to use 2 basic strategies when revising estimates: choosing between the 2 estimates and averaging them. The authors developed the probability, accuracy, redundancy (PAR) model to examine the relative effectiveness of these two strategies across judgment environments.

The trimodal pattern refers to the distribution with modes at: 0 (choosing one's own estimate), 1 (choosing the advisor's estimate) and 0.5 (averaging between the two).

However, the specific Bayesian simulation model incorporating "private information" and "own reasons" that you're asking about doesn't appear in these search results. The results focus on the empirical trimodal pattern and strategies, but don't show the particular theoretical framework or simulation approach you're asking about. You may need to access the full 2009 paper directly for the complete theoretical explanation you're seeking.

https://openalex.org/W4379966476 2023 https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000427 The autocorrelated Bayesian sampler: A rational process for probability judgments, estimates, confidence intervals, choices, confidence judgments, and response times. cit= 19
   ABS: , rather than stochastic sensory information, to make categorical decisions. This implies that human response variability arises mainly from posterior sampling rather than sensory noise. Because human hypothesis generation is serially correlated, hypothesis samples will be autocorrelated. Guided by this new problem formulation, we develop a new process, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS), which grounds autocorrelated hypothesis generation in a sophisticated sampling algorithm. The ABS provides a single mechanism that qualitatively explains many empirical effects of probability judgments, estimates, confidence intervals, choice, confidence judgments, response times, and their relationships. Our analysis demonstrates the unifying power of a perspective shift in the exploration of normative models. It also exemplifies the proposal that the "Bayesian brain" operates using samples not probabilities, and that variability in human behavior may primarily reflect computational rather than sensory noise. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved).
https://openalex.org/W2586410116 2017 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmp.2017.01.001 Sequential sampling, magnitude estimation, and the wisdom of crowds cit= 4
   ABS: Sir Francis Galton (Galton, 1907) conjectured the psychological process of magnitude estimation caused the curious distribution of judgments he observed at Plymouth in 1906. However, after he published Vox Populi, researchers narrowed their attention to the first moment of judgment distributions and its often remarkable alignment with the truth, while it became customary to explain this wisdom of crowds effect using ideas of statistics more than psychology, and without considering possible interactions with other distribution moments. Recently, however, an exploration of the cognitive foundation of judgment distributions was published (Nash, 2014). The study not only formalized a possible link between signal detection, evidence accumulation, and the shape of judgment distributions, but also in so doing, conjectured that magnitude estimation by independent individuals causes a systematic error in the wisdom of crowds indicated by judgment distribution skewness. The present study reports findings from an experiment on magnitude estimation and supports these predictions. The study moreover demonstrates that systematic errors by groups of people can be corrected using information about the judgment distribution these people together form, before errors might cause damage to decision making. In concluding, we revisit Galton’s data from the West of England Fat Stock and Poultry Exhibition in light of what we have discovered.
https://openalex.org/W4255285532 2018 https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/4we3y Averaging versus Sampling in Collaborative Judgement cit= 1
   ABS: How does a dyad combine information from different members in order to arrive at a consensus judgement? One suggestion is that groups combine information in a Bayes optimal fashion: the group calculates a weighted average of individuals' estimates, with the weightings being proportional to the quality of the information each individual possesses. Alternatively, the dyad may seek to identify which member's estimate is the best, and return that as a joint judgement. These models were tested by asking members of a dyad to make private estimates of a continuous quantity (the direction of movement of a coherent motion stimulus), and to then make a joint judgement. Joint judgements were more accurate than individual judgements, but were only partly based on optimal integration. Rather, the joint judgements were often in the neighbourhood of one of the individual judgements, or an uninformed average of the two judgements. Regression analyses suggest that dyads sampled from the alternative responses according to their initial disagreement, and their relative accuracy, on a trial-by-trial basis. Rather than learning about each others' ability, dyad members appear to rely on communication of estimated precision when forming judgements, and often resolve discrepancies by taking the best guess.
https://openalex.org/W4411610684 2025 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2025.101745 Lossy encoding of distributions in judgment under uncertainty cit= 1
   ABS: People often make judgments about uncertain facts and events, for example 'Germany will win the world cup'. Judgment under uncertainty is often studied with reference to a normative ideal according to which people should make guesses that have a high probability of being correct. According to this normative ideal, you should say that Germany will win the world cup if you think that Germany is in fact likely to win. We argue that in many cases, judgment under uncertainty is instead best conceived of as an act of lossy compression, where the goal is to efficiently encode a probability distribution, rather than express the probability of a single outcome. We test formal computational models derived from our theory, showing in four experiments that they accurately predict how people make and interpret guesses. Our account naturally explains why people dislike vacuously-correct guesses (like 'Some country will win the world cup'), and sheds light on apparently sub-optimal patterns of judgment such as the conjunction fallacy.

Based on the search results, I found the academic paper and related research on this topic:

"Where do hypotheses come from?" is a 2017 paper by Dasgupta, Schulz, and Gershman published in Cognitive Psychology, volume 96, pages 1-25.

The paper addresses an important phenomenon in human cognition. Vul and Pashler (2008) extended error analysis to the effects of averaging across multiple estimates from a single individual, finding that averaging estimates reduced error—a phenomenon they named the crowd within. However, they also found that this error reduction was less compared to the reduction obtained by averaging across individuals, with one explanation being that the error in estimates given by the same individual are not entirely independent.

The key theoretical contribution of the Dasgupta, Schulz, and Gershman paper concerns how this dependence arises. They propose that the dependence between multiple estimates arises from an autocorrelated stochastic sampling algorithm like MCMC. This is consistent with autocorrelation in hypothesis generation, as noted in prior work by Bonawitz, Denison, Gopnik, & Griffiths (2014), and Gershman, Vul, & Tenenbaum (2012).

# ABS Coverage of "Crowd Within" and Estimation Phenomena

## Crowd Within / Wisdom of Inner Crowd

The paper **does not discuss or simulate** the "crowd within" effect (Vul & Pashler 2008) or delay effects between repeated estimates.

The only relevant passage addresses **repeated sampling within a single trial**:

> "Producing confidence intervals, however, requires more than a single sample, and instead can reflect statistics of the entire set of samples: for example, the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the samples can represent a 95% confidence interval" 

This describes using multiple samples from a single posterior to construct intervals, not averaging across temporally separated judgments.

## Estimation Phenomena Covered

The ABS addresses these estimation phenomena:

1. **Anchoring effects** — "Estimates are pulled toward the boundary used in the preceding decision when the boundary is far from the correct answer"

2. **Repulsion effects** — "Estimates are pushed away from the boundary used in the preceding decision when the boundary is close to the correct answer"

I found the paper! Here's what I found about the Rauhut and Lorenz 2011 study:

The paper is titled "The wisdom of crowds in one mind: How individuals can simulate the knowledge of diverse societies to reach better decisions," published in Journal of Mathematical Psychology, volume 55, pages 191–197 (2011).

The key contribution of the paper is:

The authors address the idea that humans may simulate a diverse society in their own minds by drawing different answers from their brain. The underlying concept is that individuals can access different knowledge areas in their brain, whose joint evaluation yields better estimates than their separate consideration. The article presents a mathematical treatment of the wisdom of crowds and two potential mechanisms to quantify the wisdom of crowds in one mind.

The study analyzed new experimental data from 144 participants, which contained five consecutive estimates from the same individuals.

I found relevant research on this topic. The search results show work by the researchers you mentioned on computational models of sampling and autocorrelation.

The MC3 algorithm provides a close match to the dynamics of repeated human judgment, capturing observed long-range autocorrelations between estimates and the heavy-tailed distribution of absolute differences between successive estimates (Spicer et al., 2022b; Zhu et al., 2019, 2021; Zhu, León-Villagrá, et al., 2022).

The key condition for a sampler to reproduce qualitative model behaviors is that sampling is local and autocorrelated, with the exception of explaining cross-trial autocorrelation results which requires quantitative characterizations of the dependence in samples.

The autocorrelations of the local sampling algorithm introduce interesting effects, particularly that errors will be, on average, slower than correct responses in specific conditions, as found in human data.

The research involves Adam Sanborn, Jian-Qiao Zhu, Jake Spicer, Joakim Sundh, and Pablo León-Villagrá, who were supported by a European Research Council consolidator grant (817492-SAMPLING).

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the "inner crowd" or "crowd within" model and its relationship to delays between estimates:

According to the crowd within effect, the average of two estimates from one person tends to be more accurate than a single estimate of that person. 

Regarding the formal model and how benefits increase with delay, the benefit of spacing estimates from the inner crowd arises from the fact that estimates will be less correlated, and therefore more varied, when more time has passed between those estimates. This is explained through the diversity prediction theorem, which provides a theoretical framework for understanding this phenomenon.

The empirical support for this prediction is substantial: using proprietary data comprising 1.2 million observations from three incentivized guessing competitions, within-person aggregation improves accuracy and the method works better when there is a time delay between subsequent judgements. Additionally, the average of both guesses was more accurate than either the first or second guess alone, especially for participants who waited three weeks between guesses.

   ABS: Noise in behavior is often considered a nuisance: Although the mind aims for the best possible action, it is let down by unreliability in the sensory and response systems. Researchers often represent noise as additive, Gaussian, and independent. Yet a careful look at behavioral noise reveals a rich structure that defies easy explanation. First, in both perceptual and preferential judgments sensory and response noise may potentially play only minor roles, with most noise arising in the cognitive computations. Second, the functional form of the noise is both non-Gaussian and nonindependent, with the distribution of noise being better characterized as heavy-tailed and as having substantial long-range autocorrelations. It is possible that this structure results from brains that are, for some reason, bedeviled by a fundamental design flaw, albeit one with intriguingly distinctive characteristics. Alternatively, noise might not be a bug but a feature. Specifically, we propose that the brain approximates probabilistic inference with a local sampling algorithm, one using randomness to drive its exploration of alternative hypotheses. Reframing cognition in this way explains the rich structure of noise and leads to the surprising conclusion that noise is not a symptom of cognitive malfunction but plays a central role in underpinning human intelligence.

Interesting noise structure, termed 'stylized facts', is observed in financial markets (i.e., behaviors from many thousands of traders). Here we investigate the parallels between psychological and financial time series. In a series of three experiments (total N = 202), we successively simplified a market-based price prediction task by first removing external information, and then removing any interaction between participants. Finally, we removed any resemblance to an asset market by asking individual participants to simply reproduce temporal intervals. All three experiments reproduced the main stylized facts found in financial markets, and the robustness of the results suggests that a common cognitive-level mechanism can produce them. We identify one potential model based on mental sampling algorithms, showing how this general-purpose model might account for behavior across these very different tasks.
